Think of it this way... Why doesn't a polaroid or any other photograph get more developed after it's done? Simple. The chemical reaction is finished. This reaction of the emulsion is started by light (specifically UV light), but there's only so much reacting it can do. Once it's finished, it's finished. Just like paint can't get any drier, exposed emulsion has turned into a plastic and won't change further.

Now, I don't know a whole lot about chemistry, so I can't totally break it down for you, but that's a good starting point, I think.

The other big thing is that light is what hardens the emulsion. Water washes it away. Continued exposure would just strengthen the emulsion, not weaken it. Friction from printing will wear it away, eventually, though. It is just plastic, squished into the fabric of the screen, then dried.

From a practical standpoint, you can expose screens, wash them out, and re-expose to get them really dry. I used double exposure to get emulsion meant for oil-based inks ready for water-based inks, so it'd soak up less water from the ink while working. But necessary, but helpful.
